---
title: "Recording reading decisions as labels"
subtitle: "Create a manual annotation codebook for workforce text"
description: "Learn how people label workforce text units without pretending that judgment is automatic or neutral."
categories: [training data, annotation, workforce research]
---

The fictional Riverton Workforce Lab has 28 text units from the archived job
page and reference flyer transcript. The team must classify training offers,
application requirements, schedules, named skills, and other text.
These distinctions affect the information that workers find when comparing
notices. The team must state each label's meaning before assigning labels.

A computer cannot learn these categories until people state their meanings.
**Manual annotation** assigns labels to items according to written instructions.
Annotators must decide what each label means and apply that meaning consistently.
The task records what a text unit explicitly says.
It does not establish worker eligibility or program suitability.

::: {.callout-note}
The workforce text, labels, and research team are fictional.
The author created the examples to illustrate annotation choices without
worker or applicant records.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- describe an annotation unit and label set.
- write rules for what each label includes and excludes.
- create a versioned codebook with foundryR.
- use pilot disagreements to revise rules.
- examine ambiguous cases rather than hiding them.
- explain why a human label is a documented judgment, not automatic truth.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Decide what one label describes

The annotation unit is one source-text line. It can be a job-detail list item
or a flyer line. Each decision therefore concerns a short text that a reviewer
can examine. The `document_id` identifies the source posting or flyer.

Not all source lines are sentences. Two are capitalized headings, three are
noun phrases without verbs, and one is an imperative clause without terminal
punctuation. A rule for sentences must also explain how reviewers should label
a heading that makes no claim.

The next chunk loads readr for files and dplyr and tibble for tables.
It also loads purrr for repeated checks and stringr for text checks.
It then reads the CSV into a tibble.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)

workforce_sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

allowed_labels <- c(
  "training",
  "requirement",
  "schedule",
  "skill",
  "other"
)

first_units <- workforce_sentences |>
  select(
    sentence_id,
    document_id,
    text,
    reference_label,
    uncertainty
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  first_units,
  col.names = c(
    "Unit ID",
    "Document ID",
    "Text",
    "Reference label",
    "Uncertainty"
  ),
  caption = "The first eight manually labeled text units",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(workforce_sentences), 28L),
  identical(
    workforce_sentences$sentence_id,
    sprintf("s%03d", 1:28)
  ),
  all(workforce_sentences$reference_label %in% allowed_labels),
  !anyDuplicated(workforce_sentences$sentence_id),
  all(workforce_sentences$derived == "false"),
  all(workforce_sentences$transformation == "verbatim")
)
```

The file calls the reviewed result a **reference label**, not a ground-truth
label. The label records the reviewer's application of this codebook.
Another defensible codebook could divide the concepts differently.

### Count what the units actually are

Punctuation alone cannot establish whether a text unit is a sentence.
`Apply by October 15` is an imperative clause despite its missing full stop.
The code therefore assigns explicit grammatical categories to the six flyer
lines instead of inferring them from final characters.

```{r}
unit_shapes <- workforce_sentences |>
  mutate(
    shape = case_when(
      sentence_id %in% c("s023", "s024") ~ "heading in capitals",
      sentence_id %in% c("s025", "s026", "s027") ~ "phrase without a verb",
      sentence_id == "s028" ~ "imperative clause",
      TRUE ~ "complete sentence"
    )
  )

shape_counts <- unit_shapes |>
  count(shape, name = "units")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  shape_counts,
  col.names = c("Shape of the unit", "Units"),
  caption = "Twenty-two sentences, two headings, three phrases, one imperative clause",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(sum(shape_counts$units), 28L),
  identical(
    unit_shapes$shape[unit_shapes$sentence_id == "s028"],
    "imperative clause"
  ),
  identical(
    sum(unit_shapes$shape == "heading in capitals"),
    2L
  ),
  identical(
    sum(unit_shapes$shape == "phrase without a verb"),
    3L
  ),
  all(
    unit_shapes$document_id[
      unit_shapes$shape != "complete sentence"
    ] == "F001"
  )
)
```

Five of the 28 units are not sentences. A sixth, `Apply by October 15`, is an
imperative clause without terminal punctuation. All six come from a notice
designed for passing readers. `Paid training stipend` has no verb.
`RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE` announces an event.

Both still receive a label, and the codebook has to say how. That is the reason
the rules below talk about the unit's main explicit claim rather than the
sentence's subject.

The six flyer rows match the six-line reference transcript.
The annotation file neither expands nor interprets the source wording.

```{r}
flyer_rows <- workforce_sentences |>
  filter(document_id == "F001")
flyer_transcript <- read_lines(
  "data/workforce/training-flyer-ground-truth.txt"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  flyer_rows |>
    select(
      sentence_id,
      source_line,
      text,
      reference_label
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Unit ID",
    "Flyer line",
    "Verbatim text",
    "Reference label"
  ),
  caption = "Row-level lineage from the flyer transcript",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(flyer_rows), 6L),
  identical(length(flyer_transcript), 6L),
  identical(flyer_rows$source_line, as.character(1:6)),
  identical(flyer_rows$text, flyer_transcript)
)
```

## Write the codebook before expanding annotation

A **codebook** records the label definitions, instructions, examples, and
version. The complete instrument lives in `R/workforce-codebook.R`. Its rules
are:

- `training`: the text unit offers or describes learning, mentoring,
  certification training, or an apprenticeship.
- `requirement`: the text unit states or prefers experience, education,
  credentials, a license, a portfolio, or a physical condition.
- `schedule`: the text unit describes when work or classes occur.
- `skill`: the text unit names an ability used in the work.
- `other`: none of the four definitions applies. Headings, deadlines,
  location, work setting, and travel belong here unless the text unit
  explicitly states another category.

The text unit's main explicit claim receives one label. Reviewers do not infer a
training offer from a job title or assume that a preferred credential is
mandatory. A required shift receives `schedule` because timing is the main
claim. Reviewers mark `needs_review` when more than one label remains
defensible.

foundryR can store the codebook as a versioned object with a strict label
schema and a content hash.

```{r}
source("R/workforce-codebook.R")
annotation_codebook <- workforce_codebook()
recorded_codebook <- workforce_codebook("1.0.0")

annotation_codebook
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(
    annotation_codebook,
    "foundry_codebook"
  ),
  identical(
    annotation_codebook$version,
    "1.1.0"
  ),
  identical(recorded_codebook$version, "1.0.0"),
  !identical(annotation_codebook$hash, recorded_codebook$hash),
  identical(
    str_length(annotation_codebook$hash),
    64L
  ),
  identical(
    unclass(
      annotation_codebook$schema$
        properties$label$enum
    ),
    allowed_labels
  ),
  identical(
    unclass(
      annotation_codebook$schema$
        properties$uncertainty$enum
    ),
    c("certain", "needs_review")
  ),
  identical(
    length(annotation_codebook$examples),
    7L
  ),
  all(workforce_sentences$codebook_version == recorded_codebook$version),
  all(workforce_sentences$codebook_hash == recorded_codebook$hash),
  all(str_length(workforce_sentences$rationale) > 0),
  all(workforce_sentences$uncertainty %in% c("certain", "needs_review"))
)
```

The printed hash changes when the instructions, schema, examples, or version
changes. Version 1.1.0 corrects the unit name. The archived labels retain their
original 1.0.0 fingerprint because that version produced those records.
A new annotation run should use 1.1.0.

The code does not call an AI service. foundryR creates the measurement
instrument and calculates its fingerprint.

## Count labels without interpreting the count

A label distribution can expose a missing category or a data-entry problem.
It cannot establish how common these ideas are across the real labor market.

```{r}
label_counts <- workforce_sentences |>
  mutate(
    reference_label = factor(
      reference_label,
      levels = allowed_labels
    )
  ) |>
  count(reference_label, name = "units", .drop = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    label = as.character(reference_label),
    units
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  label_counts,
  col.names = c("Reference label", "Text units"),
  caption = "Label counts in the teaching dataset",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(sum(label_counts$units), 28L),
  identical(
    as.integer(label_counts$units),
    c(7L, 9L, 5L, 2L, 5L)
  )
)
```

The counts describe this designed example only. The author did not sample jobs
in Riverton or any real population.

## Keep ambiguity visible

Unit `s013` mentions a certificate, a word that also appears in training
offers. Its main claim is that a certificate is preferred, so version 1.1.0 of
the codebook labels it as a requirement.

```{r}
ambiguous_case <- workforce_sentences |>
  filter(sentence_id == "s013")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  ambiguous_case |>
    select(
      sentence_id,
      document_id,
      text,
      reference_label,
      uncertainty,
      rationale
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Unit ID",
    "Document ID",
    "Text",
    "Reference label",
    "Uncertainty",
    "Rationale"
  ),
  caption = "A text unit that needs the codebook rule",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(ambiguous_case), 1L),
  identical(ambiguous_case$reference_label, "requirement"),
  str_detect(ambiguous_case$text, fixed("certificate"))
)
```

A reviewer who chooses `training` may have a defensible interpretation.
The difference does not necessarily indicate carelessness.
Record the disagreement. Discuss the rule.
Issue a new codebook version if the definition changes.
Overwriting the label would remove evidence needed to improve the instrument.

## Run a pilot before labeling everything

The rules came from a pilot. Two reviewers independently labeled six units
without discussion. Their disagreements showed which instructions the
codebook needed to clarify.

```{r}
pilot_round <- tibble(
  sentence_id = c("s001", "s004", "s010", "s013", "s020", "s024"),
  reviewer_p = c(
    "training",
    "skill",
    "requirement",
    "training",
    "requirement",
    "training"
  ),
  reviewer_q = c(
    "training",
    "skill",
    "other",
    "requirement",
    "schedule",
    "other"
  )
) |>
  left_join(
    workforce_sentences |>
      select(sentence_id, text, reference_label),
    by = join_by(sentence_id)
  ) |>
  mutate(agreed = reviewer_p == reviewer_q)

pilot_agreement <- mean(pilot_round$agreed)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  pilot_round |>
    select(sentence_id, text, reviewer_p, reviewer_q, agreed),
  col.names = c(
    "Unit",
    "Text",
    "Reviewer P",
    "Reviewer Q",
    "Agreed"
  ),
  caption = "The six-unit pilot, before any rule was written",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(pilot_round), 6L),
  identical(sum(pilot_round$agreed), 2L),
  isTRUE(all.equal(pilot_agreement, 2 / 6)),
  all(!is.na(pilot_round$text)),
  identical(
    pilot_round$sentence_id[!pilot_round$agreed],
    c("s010", "s013", "s020", "s024")
  )
)
```

Two of six matched in this designed pilot. Six items cannot establish a typical
first-pass agreement rate. Here, the four disagreements show wording that
the initial instructions did not settle.

### Write one rule for each disagreement

The Lab wrote one rule per disagreement and adjudicated the four units under
those rules. A third reader conducted adjudication without participating in
the pilot labeling.

```{r}
adjudication_log <- tibble(
  sentence_id = c("s010", "s013", "s020", "s024"),
  question = c(
    "Is a preferred condition still an entry condition?",
    "Does naming a credential make a unit a training offer?",
    "Does a required shift describe timing or an entry condition?",
    "Does a heading claim what its words name?"
  ),
  rule_added = c(
    "A preference is still an entry condition.",
    "A credential that is required or preferred is not training unless learning is offered.",
    "Timing takes precedence when a shift is required.",
    "Headings are other unless the unit explicitly states another category."
  ),
  adjudicated_label = c(
    "requirement",
    "requirement",
    "schedule",
    "other"
  )
)

instructions <- annotation_codebook$instructions
rule_clauses <- c(
  "main claim states or prefers",
  "is not training",
  "schedule takes precedence",
  "Headings, deadlines, location, work setting, and travel are other"
)

adjudication_check <- adjudication_log |>
  left_join(
    workforce_sentences |>
      select(sentence_id, reference_label, uncertainty),
    by = join_by(sentence_id)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    matches_file = adjudicated_label == reference_label,
    clause_in_codebook = map_lgl(
      rule_clauses,
      \(clause) str_detect(instructions, fixed(clause))
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  adjudication_check |>
    select(sentence_id, question, rule_added, adjudicated_label, uncertainty),
  col.names = c(
    "Unit",
    "Question raised",
    "Rule written in response",
    "Decision",
    "Uncertainty kept"
  ),
  caption = "Four pilot disagreements, four rules, four recorded decisions",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(adjudication_check), 4L),
  all(adjudication_check$matches_file),
  all(adjudication_check$clause_in_codebook),
  identical(annotation_codebook$version, "1.1.0")
)
```

The current instructions contain every rule in the table.
The check reads those rules directly from the instrument.
Every adjudicated decision matches the archived label.
Those rows retain version 1.0.0. Version 1.1.0 records the corrected unit
wording for future work.

Three of the four disputed units retain `needs_review`.
The file marks `s010` as `certain`, so not every disagreement remains unresolved.
Version 1.1.0 specifies one source-text line as the annotation unit.
The historical `sentence_id` column remains a stable identifier.
Its name does not mean that every row is a grammatical sentence.

This pilot shows how disagreement can produce explicit rules.
Its six designed items cannot estimate the effect of a pilot on a larger
annotation task. They also cannot estimate the time that task would require.

## Protect the people doing the work

Manual annotation can involve sensitive, repetitive, or distressing material.
Before assigning work:

1. explain the data's purpose and permitted applications.
2. remove personal information that reviewers do not need.
3. pay fairly for reading, training, and resolution of disagreements.
4. give reviewers a way to skip harmful material.
5. separate quality feedback from surveillance.
6. record which languages and lived experience the task requires.

Expertise depends on the question. A worker, career counselor, employer, and
labor researcher may interpret the same text unit differently.
Include those perspectives in the study design rather than dismissing the
differences.

## When a language model reads the codebook too

A language model can read the codebook and propose a label for each unit.
The evidence is mixed. Models match or exceed crowd-worker performance on some
tasks. Careful replications find inconsistent performance between datasets.
Models also follow complete codebooks more consistently than category names
alone. A complete codebook contains definitions and difficult examples.

Apply the same requirements to model-label checks and human-label checks.
Record the codebook version, prompt, and model revision.
Compare a random sample with human decisions. Report the disagreements.
The guide
[Using a language model in a reproducible analysis](../using-language-models.qmd)
presents one example and a correction for the model's
errors.

## What to remember

- Annotation labels are measurements created from written rules.
- Name the unit precisely. Headings and phrases are not sentences.
- One unit per row keeps the decision small and traceable.
- A codebook needs a version, examples, and a change record.
- Run a pilot. Use disagreements to revise the rules.
- Examine ambiguity instead of making an unrecorded correction.
- Human labels require ethical working conditions and relevant expertise.
- A language model used as an annotator needs the same codebook and checks.

The Lab stated the category meanings and preserved its reading decisions.
The active-learning exercise starts with five complete job postings.
It withholds two other documents' labels from a small model during selection.
